cls: Osmotic laxative (sugar alcohol / polyol); pharmaceutical excipient and irrigation fluid
pharm: Poorly absorbed sugar alcohol that acts as a hyperosmotic agent in the gut, drawing water into the intestinal lumen to soften stool and stimulate peristalsis; also used as a sweetener, vehicle, and non-conductive genitourinary irrigation fluid.
quick: Oral laxative: 30-150 mL of 70% solution (often 30 mL); rectal enema: 120 mL of 25-30% solution
May take on empty stomach; effect is osmotic and not meal-dependent
Locally acting and poorly absorbed; generally considered acceptable when a laxative is needed
Minimal systemic absorption; considered compatible with breastfeeding
No dose adjustment for laxative use; avoid large irrigation volumes if fluid overload risk
No specific adjustment; use with caution in fructose intolerance
Bowel response, hydration/electrolytes with heavy or prolonged use
summary: Sorbitol is a poorly absorbed sugar alcohol used chiefly as an osmotic (hyperosmotic) laxative, drawing water into the bowel to relieve occasional constipation. It is given orally as a 70% solution (commonly 30 mL, up to 30-150 mL) or rectally as a 120 mL enema of 25-30% solution. Sorbitol is also widely used as a pharmaceutical excipient and sweetener and as a non-conductive irrigation/genitourinary fluid. It is not a standard FDA new-drug-approval product; dosing reflects pharmacopoeial and formulary monographs (BNF/EMA/Martindale). Historically used as the vehicle for sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), but the FDA warns this combination has caused colonic necrosis and concomitant use is not recommended. People with hereditary fructose intolerance must avoid sorbitol.
indications: Relief of occasional constipation as an osmotic laxative (oral or rectal)
Bowel evacuation / vehicle to aid passage of orally administered agents
Pharmaceutical excipient and sweetener in liquid and chewable formulations
Non-conductive irrigation fluid for transurethral/endoscopic genitourinary procedures
Historically, vehicle for sodium polystyrene sulfonate (now discouraged - see pearls)

dosage.d: 30-150 mL of 70% solution as a single dose (commonly 30 mL of 70% solution)
dosage.n: Osmotic effect; ensure adequate fluid intake

dosage.d: 120 mL of 25-30% solution as a single enema
dosage.n: Local osmotic effect in the rectum/colon

dosage.d: Approximately 2 mL/kg of 70% solution as a single dose
Historically ~20-100 mL of 70% solution as resin vehicle
dosage.n: NOT recommended - colonic necrosis risk (see pearls/contra)

admin: For oral laxative use, give the 70% solution and encourage adequate water intake
For rectal use, administer the 25-30% solution as a retention enema
Effect is osmotic - do not expect rapid relief from oral dosing (hours)
Do not co-administer as a vehicle with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (colonic necrosis risk)
Avoid entirely in patients with hereditary fructose intolerance
moa: Sorbitol is a six-carbon sugar alcohol (polyol) that is only slowly and incompletely absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. The unabsorbed sorbitol exerts a hyperosmotic effect within the intestinal lumen, drawing water into the bowel by osmosis. The increased intraluminal water softens stool, increases stool bulk and luminal volume, and promotes peristalsis, producing a laxative effect. Any absorbed sorbitol is largely metabolized in the liver (converted to fructose and then to glucose). As an excipient/irrigation fluid it acts simply as a sweetening agent, vehicle, or non-conductive osmotically active solute rather than by a pharmacologic receptor mechanism.

absolute: Bowel obstruction, ileus, or undiagnosed acute abdominal pain
relative: Concomitant use with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (colonic necrosis risk - avoid)
Active inflammatory bowel disease or compromised gut integrity
Patients prone to fluid overload (with large irrigation volumes)
monitor: Bowel response and time to effect
Hydration and electrolytes with heavy, repeated, or irrigation use

preg: Sorbitol is locally acting and only poorly absorbed from the gut, so systemic exposure is minimal. It is generally considered acceptable for occasional laxative use in pregnancy when needed, in line with bulk-forming/osmotic laxative preferences. Source data are pharmacopoeial/formulary rather than dedicated pregnancy trials.
lact: Because sorbitol is poorly absorbed and largely confined to the gut, clinically significant transfer into breast milk is not expected. It is considered compatible with breastfeeding for occasional laxative use.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for laxative use. Caution is warranted when large volumes are used as an irrigation/genitourinary fluid because absorption of irrigation solution can contribute to fluid and electrolyte shifts in patients with impaired renal function.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for laxative use. Absorbed sorbitol is metabolized hepatically (to fructose then glucose); use with caution and avoid in patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, in whom even small amounts can cause hypoglycemia and hepatic injury.

major: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) - concomitant use associated with colonic/intestinal necrosis; FDA warns against co-administration
moderate: Other laxatives - additive effect; risk of excessive diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte loss
Orally administered drugs - osmotic diarrhea may reduce absorption of co-ingested medications
minor: Other osmotically active polyols/sugars - additive gastrointestinal osmotic effect (gas, bloating)
interactions.food: Effect is osmotic and not strictly meal-dependent; large dietary intake of polyols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol) adds to gastrointestinal osmotic load.
interactions.diagnostics: Heavy or prolonged use may cause fluid/electrolyte changes detectable on serum chemistry.

serious: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance with excessive use
Colonic/intestinal necrosis when given with sodium polystyrene sulfonate
rare: Severe hypoglycemia and hepatic injury in hereditary fructose intolerance
Fluid overload/dilutional changes with large irrigation volumes (TUR syndrome-type effects)
emergency: Bowel necrosis/perforation (especially with sodium polystyrene sulfonate)
Acute metabolic crisis in fructose intolerance

monitoring: Bowel response and resolution of constipation
Signs of dehydration and electrolyte disturbance with frequent or prolonged use
Abdominal symptoms - severe pain, distension, rectal bleeding
Fluid balance and serum chemistry when used as an irrigation fluid
counsel: This medicine works by pulling water into the bowel to soften stool - drink plenty of fluids
Gas, bloating, and cramping are common and usually mild
Do not use for more than a few days for constipation without medical advice
Tell your clinician if you have hereditary fructose intolerance - you must avoid sorbitol
Seek care for severe abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, or no bowel movement after use
pk: Oral laxative effect typically within several hours; rectal effect faster
Acts locally in the gut; poorly and slowly absorbed (no meaningful systemic peak relevant to laxative effect)
Not well defined for systemic drug effect; absorbed fraction is rapidly metabolized hepatically
Effect lasts until bowel evacuation is complete
Store at room temperature; keep solution tightly closed and protected from freezing per product labeling
pearls: Sorbitol is not a standard FDA new-drug-approval product; dosing and uses here are based on BNF / EMA / pharmacopoeial monographs (Martindale, MedlinePlus, DailyMed enema products)
FDA WARNING: co-administration of sorbitol with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) has caused colonic necrosis and is not recommended
It is a poorly absorbed osmotic agent - avoid inventing precise pharmacokinetic values; the laxative action is local in the gut
Contraindicated in hereditary fructose intolerance (risk of hypoglycemia and hepatic injury)
Also used as a sweetener/excipient and as a non-conductive genitourinary irrigation fluid; excessive polyol intake commonly causes osmotic diarrhea
missed: Sorbitol is used as needed for constipation rather than on a fixed schedule, so there is no missed-dose concern. If a dose did not produce a bowel movement, do not immediately repeat large doses - seek advice if constipation persists.
overdose: Excessive sorbitol causes profuse osmotic diarrhea with abdominal cramping, which can lead to dehydration and electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypernatremia, hypokalemia). Management is supportive: stop sorbitol, rehydrate, and correct electrolytes. In hereditary fructose intolerance, even modest amounts can precipitate hypoglycemia and require urgent metabolic management.
